overview: The peak's original 1939 first-ascent line and its easiest way up: heather, talus and snowfield travel along the northeast ridge to a cirque below the east face, finished by one or two short belayed pitches of 3rd-4th class (occasionally low 5th) rock to the s

A long, sustained 15-pitch alpine rock route up the remote Northwest Face of Little Big Chief on excellent gneiss, graded IV 5.9; also known as the Falcon Route, it sees very few ascents due to its deep, cross-country approach into Summit Chief Valley.

Little Mac Spire is a minor rock pinnacle in the Southern Pickets, immediately adjacent to East McMillan Spire within the McMillan Spires group, North Cascades National Park. It is rarely climbed as a stand-alone objective — most ascents happen when parties al

face: North Face of Little Sister, rising directly above the center of the Green Creek Glacier
overview: A long, moderate alpine rock route up the North Face of Little Sister, crossing the Green Creek Glacier to gain a wide, moderate-angle face split into two aretes, then finishing with unroped scrambling to the true summit.

face: South side of Little Sister, above the 6,240+ ft col that separates it from Cinderella Peak
overview: A snow and rock gully on Little Sister's south side, reached by climbing to the col southeast of the summit and traversing onto the south aspect. It has been skied during a traverse of the whole Twin Sisters Range and climbed in winter as a moderate snow gully

face: Southeast Ridge, rising from the Cinderella-Little Sister col above the south side of the Green Creek Glacier
overview: A classic, moderate ridge line beginning at the Cinderella-Little Sister col: exposed low-5th-class climbing on excellent rock along a wild, jagged crest, finishing through looser 4th-class terrain to the summit.

face: West Face of Little Sister — the broad wall on the far side of the peak from the Green Creek Glacier, reached over the Sister Divide as part of the Green Creek Circuit
overview: The largest wall of generally sound rock in the Twin Sisters group: a long, low-commitment line of consistent 4th and low-5th-class climbing that can be soloed, simul-climbed, or pitched out over up to seven pitches.

rock_grade: Class 2-4 (mostly 2-3, short Class 3-4 moves near the summit block)
overview: This is the standard glacier line up Little Tahoma, named for the two glaciers it crosses (Fryingpan and Whitman) rather than for the east-shoulder terrain feature; modern route guides describe "Fryingpan/Whitman Glaciers" and "East Shoulder" as the same stand

rock_grade: Low 5th class (several short pitches), Class 3 on the final scramble
overview: A less-common, longer glacier approach to Little Tahoma from Paradise, crossing the Paradise, Cowlitz, and Ingraham glaciers past the Cathedral Rocks cleaver to reach the peak's south/east face, finishing up a gully-chimney and a short exposed scramble to the

rock_grade: Class 2-4 (mostly 2-3, short Class 3-4 moves near the summit block)
overview: Little Tahoma Peak (11,138 ft) is the third-highest summit in Washington and the most prominent remnant of the much larger, older Mount Rainier edifice that has since eroded away, standing as a jagged andesite pyramid on Rainier's east flank above the Fryingpa

face: South (county-line) ridge from the Sentinel Peak col
overview: A remote, seldom-visited summit on the divide between the Cascade Pass and Dome Peak country, Lizard Mountain rises above the White Rock Lakes basin along the classic Ptarmigan Traverse -- one of the North Cascades' premier glaciated high routes. Most parties

Lost Peak (8,464 ft, 1,624 ft prominence) sits in the Okanogan Range of the North Cascades, about 16 miles north of Mazama and 7 miles northwest of Big Craggy Peak, deep in the interior of the Pasayten Wilderness. It ranks among Washington's 100 highest peaks.

face: Upper Richardson Glacier to the East Ridge
overview: Luahna Peak (8,445-8,450 ft) is the second-highest summit of the Dakobed (Chiwawa) Range, immediately northwest of Clark Mountain, deep in the Boulder Creek/Napeequa River country of the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It is a rarely visited top-100 Washington peak,

An alternate approach up Luahna's southwest slope, gained via the White River side and Boulder/Clark/Luahna basins, finishing up class 2 ledges and ridge to an exposed class 3+ traverse beneath the summit and a final class 3 scramble to the top.

Luna Peak is the highest summit of the Picket Range and a coveted viewpoint over the savage skyline of the Southern and Northern Pickets. First climbed in September 1938 by Bill Cox and Will F. Thompson, it is also one of Washington's highest-prominence peaks

face: South ridge (Luna Col to the true summit)
overview: Effectively Luna Peak's standard technical line: from Luna Col/Luna Pass (reached via the Access Creek approach shared with the Southeast Slopes route), climb the broad south ridge on Class 2–3 talus to the false summit, then complete the exposed Class 3–4 tra
A short, easy final pitch of broken rock and slab to Lundin's summit from the saddle between Lundin and East Lundin, reached via a considerably longer approach over Red Pass.
A harder, more sustained line up the center of Lundin's south face, starting up an obvious hand-crack layback and finishing near the top of the West Ridge.

rock_grade: Easy 5th (Class 4 with a short low-5th crux)
overview: Lundin Peak is a jagged, three-horned summit — the westernmost horn is the true summit — on the ridge connecting Snoqualmie Mountain (6,278 ft) to Red Mountain, immediately north of Snoqualmie Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Formerly named 'Snoqualmie Lit

Begins near the low-center of the south face at an obvious layback hand-crack (5.10, can be wet). Climb up and left to gain a rising ramp, then exit rightward in the upper section on fun 5.7-5.8 rock, topping out on the west ridge near the summit. Also catalog

The original 1941 line up Lundin's south face, rising from the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek. Several low-5th-class pitches lead to a slab; the final pitch above it is steeper before topping out near the true (westernmost) summit.

face: Right side of the wall, through the Supercave feature
overview: The wall's original modern free line: a sustained 7-pitch 5.11c up the right side of M&M Wall, intersecting the huge Supercave feature at mid-height — one of the most popular and (relatively) easiest routes at the crag.

face: Lower apron of the wall, beneath the start of Ellen Pea
overview: A shorter, 3-pitch 5.11a trad route on M&M Wall reached via the Supercave approach gully; a quicker outing than the wall's big multi-pitch free lines.

face: Shares the Tiger's treed-ledge start; follows the original 1969 Langdon-Hargis line
overview: The free version of the 1969 Langdon-Hargis aid line up M&M Wall, freed in 2015 by Blake Herrington and Max Tepfer; an 8-pitch outing on immaculate granite with a sustained 5.12 crux pitch widely regarded as one of the best pitches of 5.12 on granite anywhere

An 11-pitch free line up the center of M&M Wall, widely considered one of the best free routes at Washington Pass, rivaling the Thin Red Line in quality and difficulty; climbs through a cave feature ("Tiger Belly's Lair") and a striking flake ("Tiger Flake") e

face: North face, above the head of the Yawning Glacier
overview: A glacier-approach line up Magic Mountain's north side via the Yawning Glacier, finishing with a distinct 600 ft class 4 rock face to a notch just northwest of the summit.

alpine_grade: Steep snow, 40-50 degrees (rock or snow finish)
face: Northeast face / shoulder, above the Yawning Glacier
overview: A snow line on the peak's northeast flank: follow the North Face approach up the Yawning Glacier to the Magic–Pelton Col, then take the couloir directly to the summit on rock or snow. Known to skiers as the Banana Couloir, with a documented 2,000 ft of consist
A class 4 alternative to the North Face that gains the same summit notch from the southwest side of the mountain via steep rock and an easy chimney.

face: South Ridge, gained from the col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-up Peak; summit block climbed on its NE face
overview: Set above the head of Cascade Pass near Spider-Formidable country, Magic Mountain (7,610 ft) is a rewarding scramble usually combined with a backcountry camp in the basin below. The South Ridge / Southeast Slopes standard route leaves Cascade Pass on a climber

face: Southwest cirque (north and northeast head of the cirque)
overview: A class 3-4 scramble up heathery gullies from the cirque southwest of the summit, sharing the South Ridge route's approach.

face: West face and west ridge, above the pocket glacier
overview: The technical rock line on Magic Mountain, crossing a schrund from a pocket glacier below the west face and climbing a 5.6 pitch to gain the summit ridge.

The Northwest Ice Couloir splits the northwest face of Eldorado above the wild Marble Creek Cirque, offering 2-3 long pitches (often simul-climbed) up the couloir to a flat shoulder just below the summit's famous knife-edge ridge — a steeper, more technical al
breakdown_grades: AI2-3, up to WI3 in lean conditions

overview: A shorter, 800-ft moderate rock route on solid golden granite on the eastern aspect of the North Ridge, offering a good introduction to Eldorado's alpine rock above the standard glacier approach.
A steeper snow/ice alternative to the East Ridge, climbing the face directly right of the standard route with running-belay protection, finishing at the same corniced summit ridge.

face: West Arete / west face above Marble Creek Cirque
overview: Perhaps the most spectacular alpine rock climb in the North Cascades — rises nearly 3,000 feet of continuous rock from glacier to summit. Only climbed a few times per season by very competent parties.
A moderate 4-pitch rock line up Eldorado's south ridge — a crack system to a notch, then knife-edge ridge climbing — followed by broad, mellow scrambling to the true summit.
A classic winter alpine ascent of Mount Index's Main Peak via a steep gully and exposed ridge, offering 1,900 feet of technical snow/ice climbing with significant avalanche and rockfall hazard.
